newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe economy set for six percent growth.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe economy set for six percent growth.

text.p: Falling interest rates, lower inflation, a new tariff structure and ample harvests augur well for the Zimbabwe economy which is seen growing at a rate of six percent in 1997, economists and analysts said on Wednesday.
But they warned that the picture was clouded by potential problems.

"The economy is generally going to be good. We're looking at an economic growth rate of about six percent. This is quite significant. The new tariffs, lower inflation rate, lower interest rates all help to boost the whole economy," said Danny Dube, chief economist at the Commercial Bank of Zimbabwe.
Despite two months of heavy rains, which may see estimates revised downwards, this year is still likely to reap a good harvest, the Commercial Farmers Union said.
With the majority of the people in Zimbabwe employed in agriculture, a strong season paints a bright picture for an economy already enjoying declining inflation.
Annual inflation dropped to a seven-year low of 13.9 percent last November before rising to 16.4 percent in December. January's figure was seen at 15.8 percent.
But, while inflation is perceived as being on a downward trend, it is not seen lower than 16 percent and could increase to about 19 percent in the second half of the year, Dube said.

"To get below 16 percent would be difficult. Once you look at variables like the budget deficit, it gets sticky. If the deficit was five percent we could look at inflation of 11 percent. But that will certainly not be achieved this year," Dube said.
Zimbabwe is aiming for a 1997 budget deficit of 8.5 percent of gross domestic product. The 1996 deficit was 10.1 percent of GDP gainst a target of 6.7 percent.

Analysts said that inflation could rise on the back of recent price increases in major products -- fuel, maize, soft drinks, beef -- and the new tariff structure which cut tax on industrial spares and scrapped import duty on capital goods.

The Grain Marketing Board in January raised its maize selling price by nine percent to Z$1,675 ($152) a tonne. Also in January, petrol prices rose to Z$4.55 per litre from Z$4.15, while diesel prices climbed 15 cents to Z$3.46 per litre.

"In the short-term inflation is not going to move down. The prices of several major things have gone up and the new tariffs have got to have some inflationary pressure in them," said Jason Moore, investment analyst at Dataworld.

Analysts said that electric goods, motor spares and tyres were negatively affected by the new tariffs, which raised duties on finished imported goods between 40 to 85 percent from 0-85 percent -- the highest tariffs applied including electronics.
The new structure, aimed at boosting Zimbabwe's manufacturing and industrial sectors, had the drawback of over-protection.
"The new tariff structure is trying to promote local industry but what it is actually doing is promoting industry inefficiencies at the same time," Dube said.

"Local industry is now over-protected and there is no reason why they shouldn't increase the price levels of locally produced goods to imported levels. This could fuel inflation. It will trigger a profiteering syndrome," he added.

But analysts and economists emphasised that a rise in inflation was unlikely to be substantial and would not necessarily trigger a hike in interest rates, providing the central bank was of the opinion that the trend was generally down.
